Mexicos kingpin jailbreak puts president in a hole

Mexico’s most famous fugitive may have tunnelled out of a high-security jail, but it is Enrique Peña Nieto, the country’s president, who now finds himself in a hole. Saturday night’s spectacular jailbreak by Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán — the drugs lord’s second prison escape in 15 years — is a huge setback for Mr Peña Nieto, who has cultivated a record for catching narcotics kingpins. More ON THIS STORY Mexican drug lord breaks out of jail again Analysis Mexico – the big oil sell-off ON THIS TOPIC Mexico prepares for second oil revolution FT View El Chapo’s getaway and Mexico’s oil sell-off Lucha Libre wrestles with expansion EM Squared Investors bet on Mexico and Chile Not only will it exacerbate already strained relations with law enforcement agencies in the US, it leaves the president’s commitment to cracking down on graft via a new anti-corruption system looking embarrassingly flimsy, according to political analysts. “Peña Nieto has his back against the wall now,” says Raúl Benítez, a Mexican security analyst. “This throws his new strategy against corruption in the garbage.” Speaking from Paris, where he is on a state visit, a grim-faced Mr Peña Nieto called Guzmán’s escape from the Altiplano maximum-security prison west of Mexico City, “an affront” to the nation. But his call for an investigation into whether officials helped the drugs lord flee appeared redundant: for most Mexicans, it beggars belief that Guzmán could have had a mile-long tunnel built under his shower block without at least the connivance of prison authorities. Guzmán, who was once named on Forbes magazine’s list of billionaires, bribed his way out of another top-security jail in 2001 — either in a laundry cart or disguised as a policeman, depending on which account you believe — and spent the next 13 years invisible to the authorities, although reportedly living large. His recapture in February 2014 reinforced the can-do image of Mr Peña Nieto, who has staked his presidency on a string of far-reaching structural reforms, including the historic opening up of Mexico’s oil sector to foreign investment, with the first tenders due this week. Mexican drug lord Joaquín ‘El Chapo’ Guzmán breaks out of jail again (FILES) A file handout picture released by the Attorney General of Mexico (PGR) shows the mugshot of Mexican drug trafficker Joaquin Guzman Loera, aka "el Chapo Guzman", published on the PGR website on February 22, 2014. Mexican drug lord Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman has escaped from a maximum-security prison, the government said on July 12, 2015, his second jail break in 14 years. The kingpin was last seen in the shower area of the Altiplano prison in central Mexico late on July 11 before disappearing, and "the escape of Guzman was confirmed," the National Security Commission said in a statement. There was public outrage over the apparent murder in September of 43 students by a drug gang in the pay of local police. Another scandal erupted in November over luxury homes built for the president’s wife and his finance minister by a government contractor who was part of the winning Chinese-led bid for a high-speed train project. Mr Peña Nieto has sought to take back the political initiative by focusing efforts to stamp out bribery via unprecedented scrutiny of public servants and penalties for officials and companies guilty of graft. After signing the new plan into law, the president told the Financial Times that it was a significant step forward after what he admitted was a climate of “incredulity and distrust”. But deeds have been slow to match words. An official investigation into the first lady’s mansion, for example, has yet to make any findings public. Enrique Peña Nieto, President of Mexico, is shown at the presidential compound of Los Pinos, during an interview with Jude Webber of the Financial Times.©Keith Dannemiller The escape is a huge embarrassment for Enrique Peña Nieto, Mexico's president “There has been great progress in building institutions that in the long term can probably change this trend that corruption is more the rule than the exception,” says Juan Pardinas, head of Imco, a think-tank. “But I do not see political will . . . to tackle the problems in the short term.” Mr Peña Nieto had been expected to use his state-of-the-nation speech on September 1 to relaunch his six-year presidential term. But the escape from prison of a man for whom jail appears an interlude rather than an impediment will ratchet up pressure on the president to prove he can deliver. Even in a country notorious for its far-fetched telenovelas, Saturday’s prison break by a moustachioed criminal could hardly be made up. The audacious exit was made via a ladder leading 10 metres down to a tunnel high enough for the man nicknamed “Shorty” to move along upright. Joaquín Guzmán was captured by police in 2014©AFP Joaquín Guzmán was captured by police in 2014 Stocky and surly looking, Guzmán is no Steve McQueen — even if a motorbike also played a part in the latest great escape. The lit tunnel featured a specially adapted motorcycle on rails as well as what appeared to be its own ventilation system. Tunnels are a speciality of the Sinaloa cartel boss: Guzmán is credited with pioneering their use to smuggle drugs under the US border, as well as to evade the authorities. Shortly before his recapture in 2014, he gave security forces the slip through a tunnel under the bathtub of one of his safe houses in Culiacán. Officials later found a network of tunnels connected through the city’s drainage system. FT Special Report
